paras: The lynching of John Thomas took place on 26 January 1903 near Luling, St. Charles Parish, Louisiana. Within hours of the shooting of Sheriff Lewis Oury, hundreds of armed white men chased down Thomas, a Black man accused of the killing, shot him to death and burned his body. The New-York Tribune called it the 'Horrible Revenge of a Louisiana Mob'. The story ran in papers from Louisiana to Minnesota and in one Black weekly.

According to the New Orleans Times-Democrat, Thomas, known as 'Dub', had been 'giving touble for months' at Luling, a town on the Texas and Pacific Railroad about forty miles from New Orleans. The sheriff came with a warrant charging him with assaulting another Black man with a revolver over a dice game, accompanied by Justice of the Peace L. J. Louve and two other men.

By the Times-Democrat's account, Thomas answered the order to surrender with an oath, retreated into Vioto Graziano's store and fired at the sheriff from a small kitchen at the rear. A shot struck Oury in the right temple, killing him a little after one o'clock. Wounded in the right arm in an exchange with Louve, Thomas ran to his cabin, took a Winchester rifle and headed for the woods.

The Tribune's Luling correspondent wrote that telegraph and telephone messages went out 'summoning white people to join in the chase'. Within an hour, five hundred men with rifles and shotguns were hunting him. A young man named Edmond Friloux followed him on horseback and traded rifle fire with him until Thomas took cover in a drainage ditch on the Ashton plantation. There the pursuers, among them relatives of the sheriff, shot him many times.

The body was tied to a cane wagon or roped by the neck and dragged back to his cabin. It was laid on a pile of his belongings and much of his fence, soaked in oil and set on fire. The Tribune reported that a relative of the sheriff lit the match and that pieces of Thomas's coat were handed out as souvenirs. A special train from New Orleans with a posse and bloodhounds arrived after the crowd had dispersed.

On the evening of 27 January, Gov. Heard appointed Anthony Madere sheriff of St. Charles Parish. The Weekly Iberian called the appointment 'a little hasty'. No report of an inquest, arrests or any official inquiry into the killing of Thomas appears in the coverage.

White papers treated Thomas's guilt as fact, calling him 'the murderer' and 'a negro desperado'. The Shreveport Caucasian said 'citizens' killed him after he fired on men trying to take him alive. The Times-Democrat account, reprinted in Mississippi, called Luling 'the hot-bed of negro hoodlums' and his pursuer a 'plucky young citizen'. A few papers described the killing in stronger terms: the Tribune headlined 'Horrible Revenge', the Alexandria Gazette wrote 'Retaliation was swift and horrible', and the Sun's headline read 'Murderer Lynched by a Posse'.

A Luling wire of 27 January ran in Midwestern weeklies as 'SHOT AND BURNED' or 'SHOT TO DEATH', and the Washington Evening Star summarized the Tribune dispatch. Weekly digests shortened the story further: the Willmar Tribune's digest had Thomas 'burned at the stake near New Orleans'. The Arkansas papers moved the killing to St. James Parish. The same digest line was reprinted unchanged by the Tomahawk as late as 16 April 1903.
In the Black press, the Wisconsin Weekly Advocate of 29 January ran the New Orleans wire under the headline 'LYNCH AND BURN A NEGRO' without comment. No other Black paper's coverage was found.

The papers disagreed about names: the Sun's New Orleans dispatch named the dead man 'James Jackson, a negro storekeeper', and digests called him Joe Thomas. The sheriff appears as Lewis or Louis Oury, Ory, Ourey and Benjamin Oney, although the Times-Democrat and the Tribune's Luling correspondent agree on John Thomas and Sheriff Oury of St. Charles Parish.

On the manner of death, the detailed reports say he was shot dead before his body was burned, while one digest says he was 'burned at the stake'. An Arkansas digest says he was locked in his cabin, which was then set on fire.

reader.title: Lynching of John Thomas
bases: After the sheriff was shot, a crowd of armed white men described as a mob or posse chased John Thomas, shot him to death, and burned his body (A2, A6, A7, A11).

Hundreds of armed men, named only as citizens, a mob or a posse, killed Thomas in a ditch and burned his body to avenge the sheriff's death. No report says he was taken under legal authority or tried (A2, A6, A7, A11).

The New Orleans Times-Democrat account (A6), a Tribune special from Luling (A2), a separate Luling wire (A8), the Sun's New Orleans dispatch (A1) and the Louisiana papers (A5, A11) agree on the killing of the sheriff and the shooting and burning of his alleged killer, though they differ on names and details.

accounts.label: New Orleans Times-Democrat (reprinted in Mississippi)
accounts.gist: Thomas fired on the arresting party and killed the sheriff, then fled with a Winchester. Pursuers found him in the Ashton plantation ditch and 'riddled' him with bullets, then dragged the body to his cabin and burned it on his belongings.

accounts.label: Tribune special from Luling
accounts.gist: A mob of up to a thousand men, called out by telegraph and telephone, cornered and shot Thomas on a plantation six miles away. They burned his body in a cabin, a relative of the sheriff lit the match, and his coat was cut up for souvenirs.

accounts.label: New Orleans dispatch to the Sun
accounts.gist: The sheriff's killer was 'James Jackson, a negro storekeeper'. He was captured six or seven miles from Luling and dragged back with a rope around his neck, being shot along the way.

accounts.label: Weekly news digests
accounts.gist: One digest said Thomas was 'caught by a mob and burned at the stake'. Another said a posse put a rope around his neck, locked him in his cabin and fired the house.

accounts.label: Wire story in the Black press
accounts.gist: The Wisconsin Weekly Advocate printed the New Orleans wire: a posse riddled Thomas with bullets in the drainage ditch and burned his body in his cabin.

framing.detail: The Tribune headlined 'SHOOT AND BURN NEGRO. HE MURDERED SHERIFF. Horrible Revenge of a Louisiana Mob', calling the act horrible while treating Thomas's guilt as fact.

The Times-Democrat account called Luling 'the hot-bed of negro hoodlums' and praised the 'plucky young citizen' who chased Thomas; the Shreveport Caucasian called him 'a negro desperado' and said he had fired on 'citizens' trying to take him alive.
Midwestern weeklies ran the Luling wire under 'SHOT AND BURNED' and 'SHOT TO DEATH', calling Thomas 'the murderer'.
The Louisiana Weekly Iberian reported the killing and burning without comment, and separately called the governor's quick appointment of a new sheriff 'a little hasty'.
The Wisconsin Weekly Advocate ran the New Orleans wire with no comment, under the headline 'LYNCH AND BURN A NEGRO' and the deck 'Louisiana Mob Avenges Sheriff'.

conflicts.note: The local Times-Democrat account, the Tribune's Luling special and the Louisiana weekly say John Thomas. 'Joe' appears only in digests, and 'James Jackson' only in the Sun's early dispatch.
Spelling and first name vary; the Times-Democrat and the Tribune agree on Lewis or Louis Oury.
Every dispatch from Luling and both Louisiana papers say St. Charles; St. James appears only in two digests.
